sentences.text: The Douro river was one of the most beautiful things in Portugal.
Yara had grown up looking at it from her hillside.
She had walked along its banks.
She had swum in it.
But she had never seen it from a boat, moving down it, from a distance.
It was different.
The hills were bigger than she had realized.
The vineyards were more countless than she had realized.
The bends of the river were slower.
From the boat, she could see how the whole valley was shaped — how the river had carved it over millions of years.
The hills terraced with vineyards were on both sides.
Sometimes a small stone village would appear on a distant slope.
Sometimes she saw a train going along the far bank on the little railway that followed the river.
Senhor Fonseca said almost nothing for the first three hours.
He worked.
He adjusted the sail.
He watched the wind.
He watched the current.
He steered around specific rocks that he seemed to know about.
Yara sat at the front of the boat and just looked.
She did not ask him questions.
She had promised she would be quiet.
She was keeping her promise.
Around eleven o'clock they came to the first of the big dams.
There were five dams along the Douro — huge concrete walls with locks, put in during the twentieth century.
Boats had to go through the locks.
Yara had never been through a lock before.
Senhor Fonseca radioed ahead.
They approached the lock.
The huge steel gates opened.
They sailed the little boat into a big concrete chamber.
The gates closed behind them.
The water level began to drop — the Douro was actually five long lakes, and each lock lowered you from one lake down to the next.
Yara had to hold on.
It felt strange to be in a small boat inside a huge concrete box.
When the water was fully down, the gates in front opened, and they sailed out into the next section of river, twenty meters lower than where they had been.
Yara laughed a little.
It was funny.
Senhor Fonseca smiled just a little for the first time.
He said, "Yes.
First lock is always strange.
You get used to it."
That first night they stopped at a small village called Pinhão.
Senhor Fonseca tied the boat up at the town pier.
He walked with Yara to a small pension where they had two rooms booked.
He walked her to her door.
He said, "Your room.
Lock it.
I am the next room.
If anything happens, knock hard on the wall.
We eat supper in an hour, at that café down there.
Rest." And he went to his room.
Yara went into hers.
She lay on the bed.
She was tired.
She had not realized she was tired.
She almost fell asleep.
At supper she and Senhor Fonseca sat at a small outdoor table by the river.
They ate a hot stew called cozido and drank water.
Senhor Fonseca did not talk for most of the meal.
Yara had been on the boat all day and she had been quiet all day and she wanted to talk now.
She asked, "Senhor Fonseca.
How many boats like this have you sailed." He said, "Eleven.
This one is the twelfth.
There are not many left." "Do you always sail them alone." "Yes.
Except this time." He looked at her.
"You are doing well.
I want you to know.
You have been quiet all day and you have watched.
That is what I need."
"Senhor Fonseca," Yara said.
"May I ask you something else." He nodded.
"Why do you do this.
You could have any job.
But you sail old boats to museums.
Alone.
Why." Senhor Fonseca ate for a moment.
He said, "My grandfather sailed rabelos when they still worked.
From the 1930s until the 1960s.
When the trucks and the trains took over, he was one of the last.
He was — bitter.
He thought the world had lost something when the old boats stopped.
He tried to teach me to sail one when I was your age, but there was no work in it, and I did not really care.
Then when he died, I was nineteen.
I found a lot of his notebooks.
He had written down everything about sailing rabelos — the currents, the winds at each bend, the safe places to tie up.
He had written it because he was afraid the knowledge would die with him.
I read the notebooks.
I decided he was right.
Somebody should still know.
And I have been doing this for twenty-five years now.
Not for money.
Small money.
But someone still knows how to sail these boats, because my grandfather made me care."
Yara sat with this for a moment.
She said, "Are you the only one." Senhor Fonseca said, "There are two other men in Portugal who can do it.
Both are older than me.
When I die, I hope one of them will still be alive, or I hope I will have taught someone.
I have not found anyone yet.
But — I keep looking."
On the second day Senhor Fonseca started teaching her small things.
She was allowed to hold a rope that adjusted the angle of the sail.
He showed her how to look at the surface of the water to see which way the wind was moving.
He showed her the specific spots along the river where the current would try to push the boat toward the rocks, and how to steer against it.
He talked more that day than he had the day before.
Not much more.
But more.
"Your family used to do this," he said, at one point.
"Your great-great-grandfather.
He sailed this boat down this exact river, hundreds of times, in the 1880s and 1890s.
He would have known this river the way I know it now.
It is a strange thing that you and I are the ones bringing his boat down for the last time.
It should have been him.
His grandson.
Someone in your family.
But everything gets forgotten.
So it is us." Yara thought about this.
She thought — but I am from his family.
I am doing it.
That is not exactly forgetting.
That is exactly the opposite.
But she did not say this out loud.
